slides.title: Reflections
bullets: Prepare to read, discuss and write
slides.narration: Welcome to Grade 5 English, Unit 3: Reflections. Unit 3 is called Reflections because it asks you to look closely at the world and say what you see, think and feel. You will read a rhyming river poem, three haiku and a reflective passage about the wind, and you will meet figurative language: simile, metaphor and personification. The story 'The Cracked Charter' takes the same skill into a museum mystery about a town charter with a crack running through it. The grammar focus is comparative and superlative adjectives, which you will use to compare poems, texts and ideas in your own reflective writing. In this short lecture, preview the key ideas and prepare for the independent lesson.

slides.title: What you will achieve
bullets: Identify and explain similes, metaphors and personification in poems.
Read and compare different kinds of poetry, including haiku and rhyming verse.
Count syllables and explain how poets use rhythm, sound and line length.
slides.narration: By the end of this unit, you will be able to identify and explain similes, metaphors and personification in poems. You will also read and compare different kinds of poetry, including haiku and rhyming verse. You will also count syllables and explain how poets use rhythm, sound and line length. Keep these goals in mind as you work.

slides.title: Language for precise thinking
slides.narration: Your vocabulary work begins with these words: policy, lobby, constitution, charter, legislative, mission. Listen to each pronunciation in the vocabulary lab, study its meaning in context, and use the word accurately in your own discussion and writing.

slides.title: Read critically
slides.narration: The reading sequence includes The River and Three Haiku for a Year. Read actively. Identify each text's central ideas, notice viewpoint and reliability, and support every inference with relevant evidence from the text.

slides.narration: The first language focus is What Comparatives and Superlatives Do. Comparatives and superlatives are special forms of adjectives that let you weigh one thing against another. A comparative measures exactly two things; a superlative ranks one thing against a whole group of three or more. Notice the structure in the model examples, then apply it deliberately in connected sentences and paragraphs.

slides.title: Use English for a real purpose
bullets: Explain, support and improve your ideas
slides.narration: In speaking, you will complete Speaking 1: Choral Verse Performance. Organise your ideas, use evidence and respond clearly to questions. In writing, you will plan, draft, check and revise. Use the success criteria before submitting your work.

slides.title: You are ready to begin
bullets: Activities, quiz and optional live sessions
slides.narration: You are ready to begin. Start with the vocabulary lab, continue through reading and comprehension, apply the grammar focus, and complete the speaking and writing practices. Use the AI tutor for hints and feedback any time, and bring your questions to a live session too if you join one.
